#132116. Breaking: They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2454 w)
📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: They're more complicated and more expensive than LCD screens, but your next gaming monitor should still be an OLED

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display.
  • In a recent development, likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • Sources indicate that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've said it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

In a recent development, likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

Sources indicate that the point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

In a recent development, that means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

The problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a significant, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Recent findings suggest that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to enhancement the image. Like I said, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

According to recent reports, I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

Industry observers note that the "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Recent findings suggest that pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

According to recent reports, for what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

All of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

According to recent reports, if that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a newly introduced player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

So, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

It has been revealed that indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

It has been revealed that both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

According to recent reports, over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

Recent findings suggest that however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot upcoming thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

In a recent development, in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the new PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

In a recent development, when it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint matter in bright ambient light.

Industry observers note that if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the latest RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

It has been revealed that the long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint matter. But as I peck out these words on the new 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Recent findings suggest that anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Recent findings suggest that really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The substantial brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only been out for a matter of hours, and players have already tracked down a UFO in the woods and a Bigfoot in the swamps.

Sources indicate that the UFO encounter is a random night-time event in Kelly County, on a dirt road near the Starlet Motel safehouse east of Port Gellhorn. You'll need to have finished the game's first chapter, and it's most reliable after 2am in-game.

As word spread late yesterday (18th November), it seems the event will kick off if you find a car at the side of the road with its headlights flickering, its trunk open, and clothes strewn around it. Follow the trail into the trees towards a blue glow, and you'll catch a UFO beaming down on a woman before it drops her and flies off. Head back to her car, as she requests, and the UFO returns for you. You apparently black out and come round three days later, and a bronze trophy called The Truth Is Out There should unlock.

You can seemingly trigger the event as either Jason or Lucia, and it isn't needed for 100 percent completion.

According to recent reports, and that's not the only close encounter you can expect, either. YouTuber Lazarbeam bumped into Bigfoot on the afternoon of 18th November, hours before the game rolled out in the UK, while one Reddit user reported that they weren't quite sure what they'd stumbled on, titling their post "I think I found Bigfoot".

Leonida's version of Bigfoot is actually the Skunk Ape, Florida's own swamp cryptid, and it can be found in the swamplands near Cottonmouth Lake in Mariana County as soon as free roam opens up. Listen out for a loud roar, then use Jason's tracking ability to follow it through the swamp. You may find it feeding on a deer carcass, while a second sighting has been reported south of Watson Bay.

According to recent reports, either way, the trail seemingly ends at a strange, human-like tree. Investigate it, and Jason blacks out, triggering a short cutscene in which the creature creeps up on him, as shown in this video. He later wakes near his vehicle, drenched in sweat. Save your ammo, though, as shooting at it won't do you any good.

Cryptids and aliens are, of course, something of a Rockstar tradition by this point. GTA 5's Mount Chiliad mystery kept players hunting for years, and Output Lag has already spotted two NPCs in a GTA 6 bar talking about goings-on there. Nobody has cracked a full Chiliad-style puzzle in the upcoming game yet, but I'm sure that's just a matter of when, not if.

GTA 6 launched today on PS5 and Xbox Series X/S, although some have been getting in on the action earlier as a whopping 2m Xbox players in the UK and US took advantage of the trick of changing their console's country. Even New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty. "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first.".

Eurogamer called GTA 6 an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in our five-star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

The race to port GTA 6 to PC, explained

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that revision 11/25/26 03:11 PM: One project fork, AvatarManz, now claims to run early portions of GTA 6 at 16 fps average.
  • Now that an illicit Xbox build of GTA 6 is out in the wild, anonymous modders are racing to port it to PC, and the work is progressing faster than many expected.
  • Industry observers note that what we do know for sure is that Rockstar is taking notice and has already begun cracking down on the highest-profile projects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that revision 11/25/26 03:11 PM: One project fork, AvatarManz, now claims to run early portions of GTA 6 at 16 fps average. We've updated the "top five" projects according to Portwatch VI.

Things are moving fast. Now that an illicit Xbox build of GTA 6 is out in the wild, anonymous modders are racing to port it to PC, and the work is progressing faster than many expected. At this rate, it's possible that a static recompilation of GTA 6 will run on a PC in a matter of days. It's also possible it will take much longer to produce a playable build that's actually on par with the console versions.

Industry observers note that what we do know for sure is that Rockstar is taking notice and has already begun cracking down on the highest-profile projects. As always, downloading pirated software is illegal and can infect your PC with malware, and that last bit is doubly true in the dubious AI era we now live in.

For now, the only thing to do is observe and report. Here's where things stand with GTA 6 PC ports.

Several projects have made it as rendering and playing early portions of the game at low framerates (10-16 fps average), but it's hard to verify clips making the rounds when so many are obvious fakes.

Dozens of groups of anonymous modders and vibecoders. So many, in fact, that several websites dedicated to tracking the progress of GTA 6 recomp efforts have also appeared. One of the tracker sites, Portwatch VI, has a list of projects ranked by their "playable" completion percentage—best not to take those made up figures as an accurate estimate of when a port will be complete. The top five are:.

Until very recently, the Leonida project was among those making impressive progress, but the group's creator (a 15-year-old) quit the project after Rockstar got its Discord server taken down.

Keep up to date with the most notable stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Every GTA 6 recomp project is based on the same thing: An illicit Xbox build of GTA 6 released online by Cyberleek, the notorious leaker who previously shared video of a GTA 6 development build months before its release.

With GTA 6 being the biggest game in the world at the moment and not available on PC, there is an outsized motivation to get it running.

Sources indicate that A recomp refers to static recompilation, which is the result of reverse-engineering a game's code to make it run on other hardware (usually a PC). If you want to read further on how that's achieved, PCG alum Wes Fenlon's excellent Read Only Memo newsletter has what you're looking for.

Sources indicate that as for how GTA 6 ports (and ports for other new games) are coming together so quickly, the answer is AI. The advent of AI coding tools like Claude have greatly expedited the work required to create a static recompilation of games on another platform. What used to take months to years now takes hours to days. Recomps that heavily use AI are often buggier, messier, and have fewer features than human-made fan projects, but they are fast and functional.

It's way too early to speak in absolutes, but I'm comfortable assuming that the first "playable" recomps will require an exceptionally powerful PC.

That guess is based on GTA 6 being an obviously demanding game and also some recent precedent: The earliest Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake recomps that've appeared online have high system requirements to perform as well as it does natively on Switch 2—and, well, GTA 6 has a lot more happening under the hood than a 28-year-old Zelda game.

In a recent development, that's the substantial question. My money is on no, it won't. To switch up intends on a dime would assume that Rockstar is sitting on a polished PC version that it could put out any day, and I'm not convinced that's the case. The current rumor, preceding all of this leak business, is that the PC version of GTA 6 is planned for Q1 2027 (so anytime before April).

That's not to say Rockstar couldn't expedite the process if it wanted to—they certainly have the resources to achieve the unlikely.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

World of Warcraft: Forever now has more people playing each week than World of Warcraft has seen in 15 years, according to Blizzard.

"Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years!" executive producer and World of Warcraft vice president Holly Longdale posted. "Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever!".

Longdale was quoting a post from the official World of Warcraft account, which shared a batch of "By the Numbers" stats for the fresh edition.

Since it introduced on 4th November, players have created 15,160,147 characters and 140,764 guilds, completed 1,480,343,357 quests, and defeated 9,786,925,806 enemies.

Another fun statistic for you! #WoWForever has more people playing weekly than we've seen in World of Warcraft in 15 years! Thank you all for joining us in Azeroth. We're doing this together, for Forever! 💙♾️ https://t.co/bMLQduLri2.

They've also formed 71,309,889 parties, used 28,696,386 camping items, and there have been 28,938,569 PvP kills.

Collectively, we've died a lot, too - 196,851,761 times in total, with Archmage Arugal, the final boss of Shadowfang Keep, seemingly the deadliest boss.

"You're breaking records by the day!" the post read.

Earlier this month, Blizzard said WoW: Forever was the biggest launch in World of Warcraft history by peak concurrent players, and that it had brought in the highest number of returning players the game has ever seen.

It has been revealed that longdale added at the time that it had pulled in the most upcoming players for a WoW launch in 15 years. It has since suffered its first controversy, though, with a now-fixed gold exploit.

Sources indicate that last week, players pieced together a hidden quest chain that leads to two special swords. At the time of writing, only one has been found, though progress continues in pursuit of the second.

The game has been out for just over two weeks now, and continues to prove popular among newly introduced and returning players.

#132112. Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (931 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rockpapershotgun ↗ Open Full Page

Remembering the back alley brawls of The Warriors, a Rockstar city game that isn't an open world

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives.
  • Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria.
  • According to recent reports, there's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The older I get, the more fascinated I somehow become by how videogames depict night, how particular technologies at particular times give rise to particular nightlives. I've already gushed about the Starlight Zone in Sonic the Hedgehog – the mild dissociation incubated by the soft, ceaseless glare of the construction yard, the eyeless brick at the level's nadir, the sleepless glitter of the skyline. Now, let me wind the clock forward, and backward, to Rockstar Toronto's The Warriors. One long night from the late '70s, sweaty and electric and menacing, fed through dank and sullen polygons from 2005.

Probably the best move Rockstar made with their adaptation of Walter Hill's film is to retain the element of phantasmagoria. Both the game and the movie open with a view of Coney Island's Wonder Wheel, its neon lamps forming a floating tracery of Morse code, cabins swinging almost imperceptibly against solid darkness. This is a kind of night in which light is more emblem than illumination, refusing to travel far, clinging to its source like a frightened ghost.

According to recent reports, there's a lot of demand right now for a PC version of GTA 6. I'd love a proper PC port of The Warriors, first, and not just because I like coming up with fancy ways to talk about Ferris wheels. A PC port would be a timely reminder that Rockstar used to make city games that aren't open worlds, city games made of levels, and were pretty good at it. The classic thrill of GTA is to jump into a car and circle the metropolis, radio on and arm dangling, snatches of pedestrian dialogue bursting in your wake as you zip through downtown, the skyscrapers streaming by and evaporating, the world your oyster. In The Warriors, the city is No Man's Land and the night is a tightly compartmentalised maze. Your goal is to reach the other side of it on your own two feet, before a thousand rival miscreants kick your head in.

It has been revealed that you lead a group of angry young guys of different ethnicities, wearing tribal colours and following a martial code - spiritual descendants of the stranded Greek soldiers of Xenephon's Anabais. Women barely feature in this relentlessly macho fable, and are mostly depicted as victims or seducers. Other genders are totally absent, while gay characters were considered for the film, but eventually cut. The game expands the storyline, filling in events before the titular Coney Island tearaways find themselves framed for a murder during an attempted city-wide gang uprising. But it otherwise adheres religiously to the movie's dingy and hyperbolic direction, hugging the visual language in ways that are slightly odd to return to, now that Rockstar have arguably outgrown their nerdy inferiority complex before the giants of cinema.

The game's New York is mysterious and sparsely populated: the only people abroad are other gangs and cops. The playable areas eschew affluent districts and pleasure zones; instead, you hop over a million chainlink fences in subway terminals and trashy alleyways. Most of the buildings are sealed and silent. The sky is a painted forest of chimneys, silos and stripped low cloud. You keep waiting for Batman to descend from the girders of a flyover; some of the enemy gangs certainly wouldn't look out of place in Rocksteady's Arkham. The murk isn't quite as pungent as you'd find in a PS1 flâneur like Urban Chaos, but it's respectably enveloping. I'd linger here, a plummy-accented tourist with a headful of references, cooing decorously over the stained and withdrawn shopfronts, were it not for the constant risk of getting stomped.

Back in the day, a few reviewers described The Warriors as having "deep" combat, offering a selection of directional jabs and kicks, grappling moves, terrain finishers and squad commands. I can't really see it. Certainly, The Warriors is no Sleeping Dogs. What the Warriors is is a believably chaotic brawler, with an enjoyable taste for friendly fire.

You spot a couple other Warriors surrounded by face-painted Baseball Furies, and launch into a crossbody tackle that bowls the whole group over. You straddle one of the clowns and are about to punch his teeth out when a friend lobs a trash can at the both of you. Now black-eyed and bleeding, you seize a dropped bat and swing randomly into the mob of warring outfits. Insults, taunts, chair legs and beer bottles fly back and forth. It feels like a fight. The riot spills out over each map, onto rooftops and into any businesses that have unwisely decided to stay open late. Looking back, I can see the first inklings of those spectacular drunken bar scuffles in Red Dead Redemption 2, though nobody's packing heat. The almost total absence of guns is, of course, the other thing that makes The Warriors novel, if you come to it from GTA.

In a recent development, I've yet to play Rockstar's latest GTA, which is now available on console worldwide. I've yet to decide how it fits into my evolving half-arsed anthropology of videogame nightlife. Still, I've spent a fair amount of time looking at screenshots and videos, and I'm finding the nights too bright. Too bright! All those shades seeping everywhere, all those rays being traced, all the spotlights and sequins, the way everything glimmers or glistens – it's too heady for me. Send me back to 2005's New York, where the darkness feels like it's part of the very mortar, and there's always a friend willing to "accidentally" hurl a bin at my head.

It once again goes through all the features and enhancements that will be available in the paid Switch 2 upgrade. Here's the rundown once again via the game page and official PR:.

- Support for 4K resolution in TV mode (Enhanced graphics require a TV that supports 4K resolution) - Improved performance at 60 fps - Upcoming mode: Heroes' Vault - New Hero: Shimmer - Event scenes updated to be fully voiced in English and Japanese.

In a recent development, in Xenoblade Chronicles 3 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition, you will join Noah and Mio, members of the opposing nations of Keves and Agnus, as they embark on a stirring journey through a war-torn world that harbors a dark secret. Master real-time RPG combat and enjoy newly voiced event scenes, enhanced 4K resolution in TV mode (with compatible television), full HD in handheld mode, and smoother, sharper gameplay at 60 frames per second.

According to recent reports, on this adventure, you’ll command six characters, as well as a latest mythical Hero called Shimmer – a speedy attacker who unleashes devastating rapid-fire combos and wields the power of Foresight to see the future. Lead your band against hordes of enemies, auto-attacking with each character’s distinct Arts and weapons. Pairs of characters can also Interlink to form a mighty Ouroboros capable of taking down the most threatening enemies with powerful Arts.

Industry observers note that you can also test your strength against waves of enemies in the newly introduced Heroes’ Vault mode. Here, with each enemy you defeat, you’ll power up a gauge you can use to enhance your abilities and gain additional allies. But choose wisely — you’ll need to prepare well to defeat the almighty foe awaiting you at the end of each mission!

In a recent development, once again, this Switch 2 Edition will be arriving on 3rd December 2026. Players who already have the game on Switch, can purchase the upgrade pack for $9.99 / £7.99 (or your regional equivalent) to access the newly introduced content and enhancements.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 is a technical marvel, one that's left a veteran game artist with credits on The Last of Us Part 2 Remastered and Star Wars Jedi: Survivor so stunned, he indicates he "didn't know this was possible.".

According to recent reports, del Walker is a lead character artist at Absurd Ventures who previously worked at Naughty Dog and Respawn Entertainment, and he's been giving his overwhelmingly positive thoughts on GTA 6 to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier (below). Referring specifically to the game's graphics, he notes: "Everything they're doing is what we have been told never to do in every game I've been on.".

For example, Schreier explains that during his conversation with the dev, Walker pointed to the fact that you normally only see a few characters on screen at any point with realistic hair that actually moves strand by strand, with NPCs usually made in a modular way that makes them look generic. This sort of thing comes in an effort to achieve reasonable scope and 60fps, Schreier notes.

Industry observers note that obviously, though, not only did Rockstar opt for a 30fps target on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S, but the devs went above and beyond with the detail of their NPCs, with them being individually art directed and given their own personality traits to boot. As Walker puts it, "It's like looking at a skyscraper, but I'm from the 1800s. I didn't know this was possible.".

He's not the only one impressed, of course. One game designer on The Last of Us Part 2 has called GTA 6 "the Great Pyramids of Game Development," saying that "people will be asking for centuries how it was possible and we will eventually conclude that aliens made it.".

Sources indicate that it's for good reason, of course. Even with such a lengthy development cycle and a clearly immense budget (that Rockstar won't confirm beyond saying it's not $1.5 billion), GTA 6 really is a sight to behold – there's no wonder that other devs are contemplating the sorcery behind it. As Walker so eloquently puts it, "I don't know shit about fuck. Rockstar do, clearly.".

Breaking: I’m Rolling My Eyes At Claims That Ezra Frech Losing His Prosthetic Won Him Dancing With The Stars

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dancing with the Stars' Season 35 finale just aired on the 2026 TV schedule, and congratulations are in order for Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach.
  • It has been revealed that for those who didn't watch DWTS on Tuesday, November 24, on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription, Frech's mishap came during his freestyle dance, which began with him without his prosthetic on.
  • It has been revealed that the moment received raucous applause from the in-house audience, and the judges awarded him perfect scores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dancing with the Stars' Season 35 finale just aired on the 2026 TV schedule, and congratulations are in order for Ezra Frech and Daniella Karagach. While there's no shortage of fans who are happy for the duo, there are a few disgruntled people who feel his win over Amber Glenn and others came because he lost his prosthetic during his final dance. It's a wild take that's making rounds, and I can't help but roll my eyes at it.

It has been revealed that for those who didn't watch DWTS on Tuesday, November 24, on ABC or with a Disney+ subscription, Frech's mishap came during his freestyle dance, which began with him without his prosthetic on. Frech was supposed to slip it on during a quick change segment, and while it was on when he revealed his fresh look, it quickly fell to the floor. Frech continued to dance until pro dancer Alan Bersten could retrieve the leg, and after a brief pause, Frech reattached it and completed the routine.

It has been revealed that the moment received raucous applause from the in-house audience, and the judges awarded him perfect scores. Unfortunately, comments like the one below have since been floating around X, with some arguing Frech received sympathy votes and calling fans ableist for not penalizing him for the incident:.

In a recent development, ezra wanted to be viewed the same as everyone else. Sorry but if that were the case, Amber would’ve won tonight. Ezra won cause his prosthetic fell off during his freestyle so people voted him out of sympathy & cause he was crying/bleeding after. That in itself is ableism.

I can't help but take a deep sigh when reading this take, and admittedly, I'm not the only one who has taken concern this person. With that said, if there are more people out there who quietly believe or think that Ezra's disability is what pushed him across the finish line to be the latest person to win Dancing with the Stars, let me just point out a couple of details.

To chalk Ezra Frech's win up to his final dance of the season discredits a run that was one of the best we've seen this entire season. He was never at the bottom of the leaderboard and was even at the top for a few weeks. Frech never had an off week, not once, which is the type of resilience we expect from Olympic athletes.

In a recent development, now, looking at the numbers, you'll see Amber Glenn did just as well, and even beat out Ezra for more than a few weeks. As we learned this season, however, DWTS is just as much a popularity contest as it is a dance competition. If Amber should win on scores alone, Jenna Dewan shouldn't have left, and Harry Shum Jr. would've been holding that Mirrorball trophy.

If Ezra Frech gained additional votes in Dancing with the Stars' finale after his freestyle performance, it wasn't out of sympathy. That would imply the dance fell to disaster after he lost his prosthetic, and that simply wasn't the case. Frech not only finished the dance, he completed the routine hardly missing a beat.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Tatyana Ali’s Farewell Message To Jan Ravnik Ahead Of Dancing With The Stars’ Season 35 Finale Has Me In My Feelings.

Recent findings suggest that had Connor Wood, Maura Higgins, Amber Glenn, or Tatyana Ali recovered from a disastrous moment with such poise, I feel confident the judges and audience would've reacted the same way. This is especially true on DWTS' finale night, in which I feel the judges want their scores to impact the end result as little as possible.

Industry observers note that if the fans feel Frech's win wasn't justified, then maybe it is time to push for Sharna Burgess' campaign to limit fans to only ten votes. I truly don't think it would've impacted the result at all, but that could've mitigated any perceived advantage Frech had from last-minute voters who might've used their votes otherwise.

In a recent development, in any case, I think summing up Ezra Frech's win to "losing his prosthetic" is offensive and diminishes everything else he did on DWTS. As for Amber, she also would've been a deserving winner, but let's not act like this is the first time this show has had more than one person who could've or should've won.

Dancing with the Stars has one more holiday episode on the way, but the competition is essentially done. I'm excited to tune in and eager to see what other thoughts pop up now that the season is officially over.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that cyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game rolled out, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site.
  • Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB.
  • "It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that cyberLeek, the persona of a hacker group that was responsible for leaking GTA 6 gameplay before the game rolled out, has reappeared today, claiming to have released a development build of the final version of the game on its site. This latest leak appears to be making good on a threat posted back in October, where the group stated its intent to release a full, playable build of the game.

Various social media accounts have visited the site and noted the size of the download offered by CyberLeek is, indeed 209GB. Eurogamer has seen the site and can confirm this is what the group has claimed, however I have been unable to verify the existence of any actual files. On the site, CyberLeek claims this build is from November 2026 - meaning it is very close to (if not the actual) release build. The 'executable file appears to be missing from the build, however, meaning you cannot actually - yet - get it up and running. CyberLeek is threatening to release this file at a later date, however.

"It is done," a statement from CyberLeek reads. "[Cyberleek] holds the full November 2026 build of Grand Theft Auto 6, and it is going out by torrent. Now. Every file except one. The main executable is held on a countdown." CyberLeek notes the executable will be released earlier than planned if its crypto token reaches a predetermined value. Many of the leaks to date have been related to a CyberLeek crypto scheme. Previously, it was estimated that the group cashed out at least £200,000.

In a recent development, what does all this mean? There's a very realistic chance that the game could be up and running on PC soon - undercutting Rockstar's unannounced PC release by a matter of months, if current rumours are to be believed. "This community will have it emulated inside a week, running far past 30fps," the statement continues. "[CyberLeek] told you not to preorder for a reason. This is one of the reasons.

Recent findings suggest that "If the Xbox build cannot be made to work and support holds, [CyberLeek] will work to get a PS5 build - a fallback, most likely never required. Either way: the Xbox build is going out. No double dipping for Take-Two/Rockstar." It seems these are not empty threats.

CyberLeek has been a thorn in Rockstar's side for a while now. The group initially claimed it took this action in the name of "Gamers' Rights", supposedly fighting for consumers in relation to the controversial discontinuation of game-discs and the digital-only future being pursued by game publishers. Rockstar has previously issued statements regarding the leaker, noting that the leaks are "heartbreaking" and that "this is obviously not how we intended for you to see the game after all this time". Take-Two tried to subpoena Discord for information pertaining to the leaker's identity.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada.
  • Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft have laid off 166 developers, with this latest round of cuts at the Assassin's Creed and Far Cry publishers taking place at two of their studios in Eastern Canada. Both studios affected, Ubisoft Montreal and Ubisoft Quebec, had a hand in last year's Assassin's Creed Shadows, with Montreal especially being a major and long-tenured development hub for the firm.

Both IGN and GamesIndustry.biz report that the cuts, which amount to just under 4% studios' total combined headcount, affected staff working on recently cancelled or significantly changed projects.

Industry observers note that "Ubisoft is reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations," Ubisoft said in a statement handed to both sites. "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

Industry observers note that "We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues. We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources.".

Ubisoft Montreal are presently working on Assassin’s Creed Hexe, reportedly a witchy tale set during the time of the Holy Roman Empire, which switched creative directors earlier this ear and is one of the games Ubi are keen to get out of the door. What Quebec have been up to since Shadows shipped is less clear. They're a much smaller than Montreal and were founded in 2005.

Ubisoft have been carrying out mass cuts across their studios worldwide all the way through this year. Ubisoft Singapore and Trials developers Redlynx. Ubisoft Winnipeg, Belgrade, and Barcelona. Long-time Tom Clancy studio Red Storm. Ubisoft's Paris HQ. Three German studios including Anno devs Ubisoft Mainz. All have been subjected to some form of cuts or closure.

It has been revealed that meanwhile. changes to remote working policies have also contributed to strikes at Ubisoft studios in France and Italy.

Solidarity to all of the Ubisoft workers who've been affected by these layoffs in Montreal and Quebec.

Ubisoft claims Assassin's Creed Jade is still alive as it merges two of its Creative Houses

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (655 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.
  • Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet stated mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.
  • "Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ubisoft has confirmed that while Assassin's Creed Jade - its mobile entry in the series - is still in development, its focus remains with console and PC.

Speaking during the earnings call for Ubisoft's first-half results, CFO Frédérick Duguet stated mobile was "still an opportunity for the medium to longer term, with games such as AC Jade on Assassin’s Creed", according to a transcript of the call published by Investing.com.

"Looking at what we can see in terms of long-term financial return, in the mindset of having a stronger focus in terms of capital allocation and financial returns, we consider that we would rather put our resources on bigger opportunities," Duguet said. "Today, we can say that console and PC remain our core focus for our biggest franchises.".

He added: "The focus is really to make sure that we come with strong growth on console and PC, and notably PC, which is a more dynamic platform than ever.".

Sources indicate that ubisoft last confirmed its China-set mobile game was still in the works in March, when it was mentioned in the publisher’s Assassin's Creed: Into 2026 blog. Assassin's Creed now sits within Vantage Studios, Ubisoft's joint venture with Tencent, which debuted last year.

In a recent development, ubisoft's results also confirmed some more changes to the way the manufacturer is run, with the publisher saying its new operating model is "now fully in place". Creative Houses 3 and 5 have been combined under the leadership of Julien Bares "to leverage synergies between Live experiences across platforms".

It has been revealed that all leadership roles across the Creative Houses are now filled, too. An external general manager has been appointed for Creative House 4 and is set to join in January 2027, though Ubisoft hasn't yet confirmed who. That follows September's appointment of 2K and Amazon Games veteran Christoph Hartmann to lead Creative House 2, home to The Division, Ghost Recon, and Splinter Cell, which was renamed Massive Entertainment at the same time.

Outside the Creative Houses, Motherbrain, the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI experiment Teammates, is now a subsidiary in its own right. It's working on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds". A separate unit has also been set up to look after brands that don't belong to any of the Creative Houses.

Ubisoft says the newly introduced structure is already paying off, pointing to the commercial success of Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced and renewed momentum for Rainbow Six Siege, which it says ranked among the top 10 games across Xbox and PlayStation for monthly active owners over the half.

That said, the publisher nonetheless posted a net loss of €254.5 million for the first half of the year, with net bookings down 16.5 percent to €644.7 million.

The news comes just hours after Ubisoft confirmed 166 job cuts at its Montréal and Québec City studios, the latest in a year of layoffs. They're part of the "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" that Ubisoft announced in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

In a recent development, since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

On the weekend, we learned that Ubisoft is reportedly working on a fresh Rainbow Six Vegas game 18 years after the last entry in the series.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's latest GeForce Game Ready driver, version 621.40, is out now.
  • In a recent development, which is kind of burying the lead.
  • Over the weekend Nvidia released a hotfix that supposedly caught the bug, only for owners to discover it merely delayed its onset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's latest GeForce Game Ready driver, version 621.40, is out now. "This newly introduced Game Ready Driver provides the best gaming experience for Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War 4, and Assetto Corsa Rally," the notes say, "and the addition of DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering to Where Winds Meet.".

In a recent development, which is kind of burying the lead. This patch is really a hotfix for a hotfix, an upgrade that finally addresses the bug with previous driver packages that had them pointlessly rewriting a log file over and over, rapidly adding up to tens of GB every hour and potentially damaging SSDs nobody can afford to replace any more.

Over the weekend Nvidia released a hotfix that supposedly caught the bug, only for owners to discover it merely delayed its onset. Rather than setting in immediately after a reboot, it would wait until your PC had been on for a while before shitting the bed. If you're one of the people who leaves your computer running overnight then I hope you stayed on version 621.01, the last safe driver package before the current one.

Sources indicate that forum users have been testing out version 621.40 and it seems to have not only stopped the Nvidia container service from freaking out and rewriting its log, but also caught a bug with custom cursors that would make them turn gray. Which is nice.

In a recent development, I'm tempted to play it safe and stay on my old driver anyway, though I'll enhancement for Dawn of War 4, which comes out on December 3. People with the Commander Edition can jump in early on November 30, and readers in the US and UK can enter our competition to win a Steam code for the Commander Edition right now.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upgrade [Tue 24th Nov 2026, 2:27pm]: Our sister site Push Square has also now published a guide for this Easter Egg:.

Original Story: One of the coolest things about GTA 6 since release has been watching players discover all kinds of Easter Eggs, such as the Mario-inspired hats that were shared by our sister site Nintendo Life yesterday.

We reckon this is the best one so far though - a secret portal that takes you into a nightclub from the original 2002 version of Vice City for the PS2 (which technically means it takes you back to its 1986-inspired setting).

Sources indicate that the process of getting here is long-winded, and detailed in full in the video from Dan Allen Gaming up above. In a nutshell, you have to go to the Badger R&D Radio Tower in Key Lento and use the power switch and press a button to make the Malibu logo appear on the TV. From there, visit 12 LPL substations around the map without fast-travelling, and press the correct buttons in the specific order (from the video) when you reach them. You'll then get a text, at which point you head to Reactor 2 at the LPL Turtle Head Power Station between 7pm and 6am to find the portal.

It seems someone called Memelo was the first to discover this trick:.

In a recent development, another really cool part of this Easter Egg is that when you combine all the substations together, the wording on the outside of them adds up to "Life is Passing Me By", which references a classic cheat code from the original Vice City. You actually have to use the buttons to enter this cheat code and make the portal appear.

According to recent reports, as mentioned, you get two free items for your trouble as well, which are Tommy Vercetti's classic shirt and bike from the 2002 game. These appear as soon as you're thrown out of the portal and back into the so-called real world!

In a recent development, finally, we'll also highlight that although pretty much all the footage we've seen of this Easter Egg has been exclusive to the Jason character, it does appear to work with Lucia as well. That said, we've also come across many players who claim the portal isn't showing up for them, so we're not sure what's causing it to fail in those situations.

Sources indicate that anyway, crazy stuff right?! Who knows what other insane Easter Eggs might be discovered over the coming days and weeks - some people have mentioned they're seeing a "flashback" pop-up after completing the Vice City one, with a suggestion there may be another four flashback sequences yet to be found. Let's hope so!

Have you tried this? Did you get Tommy Vercetti's items? Let us know down in the comments sectiobn below.

According to recent reports, with the sarcastic intro out the way, I will address the elephant in the room: Vovly's Adventure: Reslimed is out today too. In a recent development, keepsake Country was supposed to release earlier this month, but seemingly got caught up in the backlog Valve are faced with that's undoubtedly been caused by genAI games. In any case, the burgle-em-up does look quite delightful. I'm not sure if I can quite put my finger on exactly why I get this feeling, but it calls to mind a more complex version of the kind of game you'd find on Cartoon Network's website back in the day (which is a high point of praise, I'd like to be clear).

Sources indicate that each house in Keepsake Country is procedurally generated, meaning you never quite know what to expect when you enter. There's lockpicking, resident tie upping, and of course stealing to be done, but it doesn't just stop at the house. Parking your car, for instance, is an important thing to consider; do you want it hidden so you're less likely to be discovered, or right at the front door so you can make a speedy escape? Not to mention you have to deal with the fuzz showing up at some point if you aren't quick enough!

It has been revealed that gear and the like can be improved between runs, meaning you can lockpick faster or delay the cops, it all seems quite systemically thoughtful. Very much some immersive sim vibes from this one, just on a much smaller scale. And most certainly worth considering picking up on a release day like today! If you're interested in doing so, you can pick it up on Steam right here.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With World of Warcraft: Forever's first raids set to release in early December, developers of the game have spoken about endgame itemisation and their desire to disrupt the "best-in-slot" (BIS) mindset that's been at the core of WoW's progression for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that this information stems from the latest episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast.
  • In a recent development, "I essentially want to get rid of BIS," Moon noted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With World of Warcraft: Forever's first raids set to release in early December, developers of the game have spoken about endgame itemisation and their desire to disrupt the "best-in-slot" (BIS) mindset that's been at the core of WoW's progression for years.

Recent findings suggest that this information stems from the latest episode of the official World of Warcraft: Forever podcast. In it, senior game designer Aidan Moon revealed his philosophy around the game's itemisation, which he played - and plays - a major role in designing.

In a recent development, "I essentially want to get rid of BIS," Moon noted. "I think BIS is not a good thing for a video game that's supposed to be about role-playing. That's why I've introduced the creature subtype system, where things are more effective against murlocs [for example]. We've introduced the biome system too, and in the raid it's different.".

He gave an example from upcoming raid Barrow Deeps, which will be split into different biomes that offer opportunities for such creature subtype gear to be put to use. "If you go to the left wing that's snowy; if you go to the right wing, that's haunted; if you go down below, that's cavernous. ... I think your BIS should be different for every single boss if you're making a theoretical BIS list.".

It has been revealed that moon acknowledged that the system is open for players to interact with to the extent they're comfortable with. Some players might bring optimised gear for certain bosses, while others might not, opting instead for generally good gear to perform well regardless of the fight.

According to recent reports, it's an excitingly different approach that goes against the established norms of WoW's endgame raiding. In other versions in World of Warcraft, gear progression is more linear: people go into raids with an idea of what gear drops are best for their character, and intentionally hunt these pieces to replace the set they're wearing. It's a vertical sense of progression. Will theoretically having multiple sets of equipment, for multiple situations, change this?

Best-in-slot gear is an especially pertinent topic in WoW Forever at the moment, given the most dedicated players are reaching max level, or nearing it, and are hunting for items in preparation for the upcoming raid. I'm right now ticking off equipment from a best-in-slot list for a Balance Druid. Whether this player behavior will change when the changes are implemented remains to be seen. Perhaps the approach will expand, with players continuing to hunt down generally accepted 'good' items while also seeking side pieces that provide situational bonuses along the way.

The Blizzard discussion on raid itemisation went beyond standard power items. Chase items, those with especially low drop rates, were also talked about by Moon, noting that Barrow Deeps continues several such items that he hopes will keep players returning to it for years to come.

The items Moon is likely referring to here probably relate to mounts, pets, situational gear, and perhaps campfire bonuses.

For example, I obtained an upgraded campfire earlier in the game that allows a greater campfire to be built that allows more buff items to be placed around it.This has essentially locked me in as a campfire slave for the upcoming raid tier, and valuable to a raid composition.

In a recent development, world of Warcraft: Forever has proven extremely popular since its early November release. The game broke franchise records for Blizzard on launch, and has more weekly players than WoW has seen in 15 years. Judging from early impressions of World of Warcraft: Forever, the game has real merit.

  • He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I've been looking forward to seeing Sir Patrick Stewart return as Professor Charles Xavier in Avengers: Doomsday, especially knowing he'll be sharing the screen with Sir Ian McKellen again. The two actors have been part of the X-Men franchise for more than 25 years, and I can't imagine the flick without them. Although after Stewart's death in October, his final appearance will carry considerably more emotional weight than anyone originally anticipated. Now Marvel Studios president Kevin Feige and directors Joe and Anthony Russo are opening up about Stewart's last day on set for the upcoming Marvel movie, and I'm already getting emotional.

Sources indicate that speaking with Entertainment Weekly, Feige recalled a moment when the legendary actor addressed the crew after completing his work. Nobody knew for certain what it would mean at the time, but looking back, it sounds like Stewart knew he was saying goodbye. Marvel's head honcho revealed:.

He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew. We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was.

Industry observers note that well, that got me. Stewart died at 86 on Oct. 29, making Doomsday his final on-screen performance. Knowing he apparently recognized the significance of that moment makes the story particularly heartbreaking.

It has been revealed that I've always admired Stewart's ability to bring such extraordinary warmth and humanity to Charles Xavier. Even when the X-Men movies weren't particularly great, his presence could make a scene work. There's something incredibly moving about imagining the actor who spent decades portraying a mentor taking a moment to address the people who helped bring his final performance to life. Anthony Russo admitted that Stewart's farewell carried a weight that everyone seemed to recognize, even if nobody wanted to acknowledge what it might mean:.

I think it was in the back of all of our heads, we may never see him on set again.

According to recent reports, the director also revealed that Stewart was dealing with significant health challenges while filming. According to Russo, the actor's determination to deliver the performance was evident to everyone around him. And it wasn't easy watching someone they admired push himself so hard. He continued:.

It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence — for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew. You could see it wasn’t just the effort of a regular actor showing up and delivering that kind of presence and performance and experience for others, collaboration. It was someone who was really being challenged in a very deep way on a health level, showing up and doing that. For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.

I have a feeling that sentiment will carry over to audiences when the film finally arrives. Stewart first portrayed Xavier in the 2000s X-Men, eventually becoming one of the franchise's most recognizable faces. He returned for several sequels, delivered a particularly devastating performance in 2017's Logan, and later surprised MCU fans with an appearance in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness.

Now, more than a quarter-century after his first appearance, he'll be returning alongside McKellen's Magneto. Joe Russo revealed that the longtime friends share an emotional scene about forgiveness, which could be especially difficult to watch under the circumstances.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that another detail from the interview makes this farewell even sadder. Stewart was reportedly offered a role in Avengers: Secret Wars as well, but chose to appear only in Doomsday. Feige also confirmed that Marvel is working on a tribute to the actor for the upcoming release.

It has been revealed that I can't help thinking about how many people grew up with Stewart's Professor X, myself included. His portrayal helped define what upcoming superhero movies could accomplish emotionally long before cinematic universes became the norm.

According to recent reports, knowing his final day involved such a heartfelt farewell to the people around him makes me appreciate his commitment even more. Whatever happens to Charles Xavier in Doomsday, I'm grateful Stewart got one last opportunity to play him.

Avengers: Doomsday arrives in theaters December 18 as part of the 2026 movie release schedule. I'll be bringing tissues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

GTA 6 has notably introduced without a PC release, landing on PlayStation 5 and the Xbox Series X|S only – a debacle that has, of course, led to fans attempting to get the Grand Theft Auto entry running on computers.

According to recent reports, there are various "projects," so to speak, attempting to tackle an unofficial PC port – but one in particular made rounds recently after Rockstar allegedly took its Discord server down and prompted its lead – an anonymous 15-year-old (as per their own words) – to say "goodbye," noting that "managing school and sports is hard enough without having middle-aged men yell and complain to you on Discord." Well, they're back… and so is their project, Leonida. And, according to a new post on Twitter from "NotRexed," the Leonida lead, they'll provide more information on their supposed GTA 6 PC port in the coming days. "Leonida is NOT dead," they write. "I have been doing a lot of work behind the scenes. I'll have some stuff to show all of you soon." They follow up on this with a response stating that Leonida should feature "native Linux support," with "more on that later.".

According to recent reports, obviously, it's difficult to verify anything they say, seeing as this is a (very) unofficial port, should it be happening at all. Rockstar itself hasn't actually spoken on the matter publicly. It all stemmed from notorious GTA 6 leaker "Cyberleek," who recently uploaded an executable file and the Xbox build of the game online. Shortly after, fans like NotRexed picked it up and began working toward a PC version of Grand Theft Auto 6.

I'm not so sure what'll happen from here, but I am personally left wondering when Rockstar will announce an official PC release of the game. It's no small launch, after all, smashing records as the highest-rated game of all time on Metacritic and proving "the biggest launch in PlayStation history" (with Sony reporting "more than 39 million unique players" playing on the PS5 alone). Imagine how those numbers could grow….

It has been revealed that I'm a reasonable man. I don't expect every PS1-styled, cosmic horror, nakedly Alien: Resurrection-homaging retro FPS to suffocate me under a blanket of misery. Some of the lighter moments in Derelikt, which released last week, even land: I was grinning my cheeks off as I gorged on the Eldtrich knowledge sealed within an alien obelisk, while repeatedly hanging up on the aghast scientist who kept videocalling me to stop.

In a recent development, still, Derelikt is fortunate that it's a good shooter, as it often gets muddled on whether it wants to be a horror game as well. It certainly threatens the spooks, trapping you in an oppressively dingy asteroid rig in the orbit of Saturn - the scariest of the ringed gas giants! - and warping most of the other staff into vaguely echinodemic monsterpeople. Also, opening the inventory reveals it to be made of rectangles, a classic symptom of a video game character about to get mangled in the nerves and face.

But nah, shotgun go boom boom. It turns out Derelikt's derelict dwellers are both perfectly susceptible to mundane lead, and sparing customers of ambush tactics at most; several even stand around with their backs turned, as if waiting for you to surprise them with a lethal pipe swing. And, even on Medium difficulty, the opening spell of fight-or-run scarcity rapidly gives way to an abundance of ammo and health pickups that can easily fill the pocket grid to bursting. I don't claim to have been playing perfectly, but I'm about halfway through and the only way I see myself running low on bullets is if I start using them to punch the complete works of Thomas Campion into a wall.

Industry observers note that it's indecisive tonally, as well. The dialogue, and there are a fair few survivors to chat with, seems interested in emulating the gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style of Upcoming Millennium action game scripts. Which I can sort of see the logic behind, given the visuals and sound design also, and arguably much more painstakingly, mimic that era. But the downside remains that it ends up with a gravitas-starved, "Woah man" style, just with an extra dash of sideways-winking awareness. Again, it only sometimes works, and it's never scary or eerie. But then there are also more earnest attempts to spin uneasiness, with pages of deranged scribbles left behind by the dwindling crew, and at least a couple of genre-classic wall daubings, which tend to leave me wishing developers Visuwyg had just picked a lane.

It has been revealed that again, though, underneath all the smartarsing is a quality little shooter. The retro presentation does little to soften the heavy, industrial kick of its gunfire, and although many of the meatier freaks are more absorbent than they look, their pained thrashing really helps sell the impact of every individual shot. I also don't really mind the lack of Dead Spacey surprise attacks, as the station's narrow confines tend to force you into tenser, close-range encounters in an organic way anyhow.

Sources indicate that more impressive still is how Derelikt manages to fabricate a cold, apprehensive atmosphere befitting its fallen space base, in direct defiance of its own quasi-comedic script. This is mainly thanks to the clanging, low-lit station itself, which teases you with just enough flashes of comfort – a stretch of marble floor here, a messy rec room there – to make your quick return to its steel guts feel all the more unpleasant. Some credit must also go to the puzzling, the cardkey hunts and code searches of which initially had me fearful of the more obstinate, opaque, classic horror style preferred by fellow backwards-looker Silver Pines. Instead, it's more like a compacted Deus Ex, hinting at the need to peek at people's computers and scour the environments for the needed codes. Which makes for generally smoother progress, yes, but also gets you more involved and present inside Derelikt's infested walls.

Midway-through impressions, then: it's a little silly, and perhaps a little confused, but Derelikt finds its focus whenever something needs making dead. I shall continue blasting xenos and burning my eyes out with magic rocks until – no, madam, please hold – further notice.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Capcom has confirmed it'll be delisting its multiplayer dinosaur shooter Exoprimal in March 2027, and then turning the game's servers off in September.

The news comes from an "end of service announcement" published on the official Exoprimal website, where it is remarked: "We cannot thank you enough for the love and support you have shown over the years, and we sincerely apologize for the gravity of this announcement.".

As of today, 25th November 2026, the game's four Survival Passes have already been taken off the PS Store.

Then, on 30th March 2027, Exoprimal and all its DLC and any other content will be removed from all storefronts.

Finally, the "end of service" phase and complete shutdown of Exoprimal is scheduled for 29th September 2027.

Recent findings suggest that "Exoprimal will no longer be playable after the end of service," Capcom confirms. While the game did receive a physical release on a disc, it requires an internet connection to servers in order to play. With those gone, Exoprimal will stop functioning no matter whether you own it physically or digitally.

In a recent development, capcom has enjoyed an incredible PS5 generation with multiple critically-acclaimed releases, but Exoprimal is one of the few titles it put out that fell below the standards it set. That's not to say Exoprimal was bad, though — far from it.

In our own Exoprimal PS5 review, we awarded it a 7/10 and called it a "white-knuckle fusion of Overwatch and Gears of War". However, competition in the multiplayer space is strong, and it appears the game didn't do enough to sustain a significant enough playerbase for Capcom to justify keeping the servers turned on.

Now, in less than a year, Exoprimal will be delisted and rendered completely unplayable.

The game is still full price on the PS Store, but between now and March 2027 (when the delisting occurs), I do imagine Capcom will hand it some steep discounts so those still curious can try it for cheap.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that valve giveth, and Valve taketh away in their latest Steam Machine availability upgrade. The dinky SteamOS PC continues to have a terrible time with AI industry-inflicted hardware parts shortages, which at least for its flagship 2TB model, have become such a problem that Valve are suspending new orders until further notice. While Valve's post states that they "have wrapped up sending purchase invites out to all remaining 2TB reservation holders" – meaning if you'd previously reserved one, you'll still get your chance to buy – "supply restraints" have put the kibosh on any new orders for now.

It's not all bad news, though. The cheaper 512GB Steam Machine has achieved "add-to-cart status", which is Valve's slightly odd way of saying you can snap one up without having to join a reservation waitlist. Just like in the Before Times! The post does add that 512GB stock is still limited, so that might sell out too if they can't source enough parts to build fresh ones, though this is still the first time that the refreshed Steam Machine has been waitlist-free since launching in June.

One could, with the aid of a Torx screwdriver and a conveniently illustrated guide, work around the 2TB model's lack of existence by nabbing a readily available 512GB Machine and replacing its stock SSD with a chunkier aftermarket drive. A not-terrible, budget two-gigster can be had from £240, which when added to the 512GB Machine's £879 outlay, actually works out a little less than buying a 2TB Machine as is. SteamOS is free to download and install, and swapping out the Steam Machine's SSD is considerably easier than the plasticky brain surgery of Steam Deck drive replacement.

It has been revealed that of course, ideally none of that would be necessary, and we could all fill our living rooms with sub-£700 Steam Machines that had never been choked by the greedy hands of industrial-scale RAM hoarders. But that's not the world we live in. Indeed, Valve end the post by rather chillingly suggesting that their hardware prices may rise yet again.

"We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units," they say, "but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels; as a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.".

"We anticipate having more information to share come January.".
